blocks.text: A candidate writes to the Principal: 'Abeg, I wan fade from boarding house because the food no dey.' The facts may be true. The letter still fails. Nigerian Pidgin and school slang are living languages, but they are not the language of a formal letter in WAEC or NECO. Audience decides the register, and a principal is not a classmate.

blocks.markdown:
Usage sits on a scale, not a switch.

- **Formal / Standard English** — complete sentences, no slang, no contractions in official writing, exact vocabulary. Letters to a principal, a commissioner, an examiner.
- **Colloquial** — relaxed but still English: contractions, everyday words, a personal tone. A letter to a friend, a speech to classmates.
- **Slang** — in-group words that fall out of date quickly: *fade* (leave), *chop* (eat or embezzle), *gist* (news), *wahala* (trouble).
- **Nigerian Pidgin** — a full language with its own grammar (*I dey go*, *e no easy*), not broken English. It is appropriate in the market and among friends. It is not appropriate in the composition paper unless the rubric asks you to represent speech.

blocks.title: Pidgin is not Standard English with mistakes
blocks.text: I dey come is grammatical Pidgin. It is not a failed attempt at I am coming. The examination error is not that Pidgin exists; it is that a candidate used Pidgin where the audience — a principal, an examiner, a newspaper reader — requires Standard English.

rows: I want to leave / I intend to go
There is not enough food / the meals are inadequate
It is not easy / the situation is difficult
She has embezzled the money / she has spent the money
Tell me what happened / give me the news
I shall see you / I will see you
blocks.caption: Raising informal Nigerian usage to Standard English

items: **Principal, commissioner, examiner, editor** — formal Standard English: no slang, no Pidgin, no *abeg*, no contractions in letters.
**Parent you respect but know well** — polite Standard English, a little warmth allowed.
**Classmate or sibling** — colloquial English is expected in an informal letter; Pidgin and heavy slang still cost marks unless used briefly as quoted speech.
**Junior students in an assembly speech** — simple Standard English, direct address, still no slang in the script you submit.
When in doubt, write the Standard English and keep any Pidgin inside inverted commas as something a character said.

blocks.title: Rewriting for the principal
blocks.prompt: Rewrite in Standard English for a letter to the Principal: 'Abeg, I wan fade from boarding house because the food no dey and wahala too much.'

steps.text: Identify the audience: the Principal, so the target is formal Standard English.
Abeg → Please, or drop it and let the request carry the courtesy.
I wan fade → I wish to withdraw from the boarding house / I should like to leave the hostel.
the food no dey → the meals are inadequate / there is often not enough food.
wahala too much → conditions have become very difficult / the situation has become intolerable.
Join into two formal sentences: 'I wish to withdraw from the boarding house because the meals are inadequate. Conditions have become very difficult.'

blocks.answer: I wish to withdraw from the boarding house because the meals are inadequate and living conditions have become very difficult.

blocks.title: WAEC and NECO tip
blocks.text: Before you write a word, name the audience in the margin: principal, friend, newspaper, junior assembly. Then forbid yourself anything that audience would not accept. Slang such as fade, gist and wahala is a register mark lost in a formal letter and only barely tolerated in an informal one. Pidgin in an official letter is a collapse of register, not a mark of local colour.

points: Usage ranges from formal Standard English through colloquial English to slang and Pidgin.
Nigerian Pidgin is a language in its own right; it is still the wrong choice for official examination writing.
Slang such as fade, gist and wahala must be rewritten for a principal or an examiner.
Audience decides the register: principal versus classmate is the classic contrast.
A rewrite keeps the meaning and raises the formality; it does not add new facts.
